summary: Intravenous fluid therapy is a cornerstone of optimizing body hydration, circulation, and perfusion, yet its rational implementation is limited by inconsistent clinical terminology. As fluid therapy moves toward AI-empowered clinical decision support systems (AI-CDSS), there is a critical need for high-quality, verified training data. The reliability of these systems is currently threatened by misleading data resulting from ambiguous definitions and the interchangeable use of nonsynonymous terms, such as “dehydration” and “hypovolemia.” This multidisciplinary panel-of-experts opinion article intends to start a discussion by identifying the key drawbacks in current terminology and proposes solutions, including a shift toward adequacy-based phenotypes and categorizing blood and water volumes as “insufficient,” “optimal,” or “excessive” rather than relying on context-sensitive quantitative measures such as “low,” “normal,” or “high.” Illustrative scenarios are used to show how inconsistent terminology and static quantitative labels could mislead an AI-CDSS. The proposed phenotype matrix is designed to provide a structured, systematic description of fluid requirements for specific clinical objectives that can be integrated into clinical algorithms and machine learning databases. An example of a fluid requirement assessment algorithm is used for exploring its applicability in AI training. The proposed terminology and phenotype matrix are provisional: they represent the opinion of a multidisciplinary expert panel and have not undergone formal consensus, clinical validation, or testing within an AI system. Broad consensus-building initiatives will follow.
title: Revising Terminology and Phenotype Definitions for AI-Based Decision Support in Fluid Therapy: Call for Consensus

summary: Clinical large language model agents depend on both model capability and the surrounding system that selects information, constrains actions, and verifies execution. In this Viewpoint, we argue that this harness should be an explicit unit of clinical agent design, evaluation, and reporting. Our aim is to help clinical informatics and development teams specify this layer and to help evaluators and institutional governance teams assess its contributions and risks. Selected benchmarks show substantial performance differences across harness configurations, but architecture comparisons, bundled improvements, and within-model component comparisons support different levels of causal attribution. We propose a revisable 3-tier framework: tier 1 specifies general orchestration functions, including prompts, tools, output schemas, control flow, memory, and generic verification; tier 2 specifies their clinical adaptations for knowledge integration, differential reasoning, missingness and temporality, safety verification, and workflow alignment; and tier 3 specifies a failure-driven evaluation cycle applied to both. Our contribution is a framework that makes these connections explicit. We provide classification rules, an illustrative clinical example, a proposed evaluation protocol, and a minimum reporting checklist. Observable execution traces are distinguished from private model reasoning, with provenance and privacy safeguards supporting retrospective reconstruction. Evaluation should separate task success, clinical correctness, process safety, and operational reliability. Lightweight fine-tuning can complement harness design; their interaction requires controlled study. The framework is a proposal for empirical testing, not a validated taxonomy or evidence of deployment safety.
title: Beyond Model Choice: A Harness-Centered Framework for Designing Clinical Large Language Model Agents

summary: AI-enabled digital medicine platforms in Europe are developed within overlapping rules for personal data, medical devices, AI, clinical research, health data access, and health technology assessment. This viewpoint represents the authors’ experience and interpretation from the preimplementation phase of INTERCEPT, an Innovative Health Initiative consortium that plans to validate biomarkers and develop a blood-based risk score for early Crohn disease interception. It does not report original empirical research, a systematic regulatory review, a deployed platform, or a validated AI model. Our aim is to explain how compliance-by-design can be translated into an auditable governance architecture and to identify what still requires scientific evaluation. We advance 3 messages. First, governance must begin with intended purpose and boundary mapping: a digital platform may contain research, operational, and medical device software functions, and conformity of one module cannot be inferred for the platform as a whole. Second, overlapping obligations can be operationalized through 5 linked controls: modular responsibility and change control, federated data governance, traceable AI life cycle management, consent and participant rights orchestration, and a common cross-border governance core with local adaptations. Third, compliance is not a surrogate for model validity, clinical benefit, trust, scalability, or market access. Before clinical deployment, planned AI components require prespecified labels and cohorts, leakage prevention, missing data and imbalance strategies, calibration, subgroup assessment, external validation, human factors evaluation, and postdeployment algorithmovigilance. A hypothetical biomarker risk score update illustrates how the 5 controls interact. INTERCEPT is informative because it combines cross-border biomarker research, planned predictive analytics, and heterogeneous institutional settings while key design decisions remain modifiable. Its contribution is nevertheless conceptual: the proposed framework is a testable governance hypothesis, not evidence of implementation success. Prospective studies should compare it with alternative governance models and assess safety, workload, participant experience, evidence generation, and regulatory performance.
title: Compliance-by-Design in an AI-Enabled Platform for Early Crohn Disease Interception: A Viewpoint

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> The proliferation of electronic clinical information resources has transformed how evidence is accessed during primary care consultations, particularly in community settings where clinicians must rapidly access reliable information at the point of care (POC). For general practice trainees, who are still developing clinical expertise and information-seeking skills, how these digital resources are used during real-time decision-making remains poorly understood. <strong>Objective:</strong> This study aims to investigate the selection, use, and real-time interaction with electronic clinical information resources used by Australian general practice (GP) trainees (specialist vocational trainees in family medicine) during clinical decision-making. <strong>Methods:</strong> Using a novel qualitative interview and screen-capture approach, this study combines semistructured interviews with a screen-recorded, think-aloud protocol capturing real-time interaction with digital information systems. In 2024, a total of 20 GP trainees (women: n=13; men: n=7) in their final 2 years of GP specialty training participated in the study, first discussing their general approaches to information seeking, followed by a live, video-recorded task session where participants engaged with hypothetical clinical vignettes using their usual information resources. Data were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. GP trainees from various community-based training practices across Australia were purposively sampled to capture diverse perspectives within primary care settings. <strong>Results:</strong> GP trainees relied on a combination of personal knowledge, clinical guidelines, and electronic information resources during decision-making. Major themes included a desire to “do the right thing” while under constraints of other themes such as time limits and perceived patient perception. Think-aloud sessions revealed common patterns in information resource selection, and that trainees often struggled with the efficiency and accessibility of finding specific information. Trainees sometimes made errors in information synthesis and judgment. Trainees frequently used a stepped approach to choosing internet resources and preferred resources that provided quick, reliable answers, indicating a preference for accessible information resources over comprehensive but time-consuming evidence repositories. <strong>Conclusions:</strong> Trainees used rapid, pragmatic strategies centered on trusted resources to support decision-making within significant time and contextual constraints. While trainees endorsed the principles of evidence-based medicine, the realities of POC practice limited direct engagement with the underlying evidence base. These findings suggest that current electronic clinical resources may require redesign to better integrate with clinical workflows and present clinically relevant evidence in ways that support timely, evidence-informed decision-making in primary care.
title: The Use of Electronic Information Resources by General Practice Trainees During Consultations in Australia: Qualitative Analysis of Interview and Screen-Recording Data

summary: In response to a recently published Delphi study on AI in spiritual care, this commentary focuses on ways to perceive the relationship between AI and human beings in the context of spiritual care. We explore this relationship by framing it within the philosophy of Martin Buber. Because AI has no lived experience or existential crises of its own, we question whether a truly fulfilling encounter between a human being and an AI model is possible when the relationship is inherently asymmetrical on an existential level.
title: Relating to AI in Spiritual Care

summary: Background: Machine learning models are increasingly used for glycemic event prediction and continuous glucose forecasting, but targets, populations, horizons, validation, and uncertainty reporting remain heterogeneous. Objective: This study aimed to evaluate machine learning models for glycemic prediction in type 1, type 2, and mixed diabetes populations while distinguishing the full evidence map from the quantitatively analyzable subset. Methods: We searched 9 English- and Chinese-language databases from inception to April 12, 2026, for studies predicting future glycemic events or glucose values in people with diabetes. Continuous forecasting and binary event prediction were analyzed separately. Root-mean-square error (RMSE) was the principal continuous end point; mean absolute error was supportive. Area under the receiver operating characteristic curve was synthesized using a Bayesian random-effects model because analyzable 2×2 data were sparse. Two reviewers (HY and DA) independently applied PROBAST (Prediction Model Risk of Bias Assessment Tool) to 19 quantitative-source reports (28 assessment units). Results: We identified 787 records, assessed 310 full texts, and included 299 reports representing 270 studies; 19 reports contributed to quantitative synthesis. The review included 128 type 1, 26 type 2, 78 mixed, and 38 unclear-diabetes-type studies. Pooled RMSE was 1.18 mmol/L (95% CI 1.01‐1.34; 37 effects), supportive mean absolute error was 0.90 mmol/L (95% CI 0.78‐1.02; 20 effects), and Bayesian pooled area under the receiver operating characteristic curve was 0.926 (95% credible interval 0.877‐0.957). Supportive sensitivity and specificity were 0.77 and 0.80. Of 28 PROBAST units, 24 were high risk, 2 unclear, and 2 low. Post hoc exploratory within-report analysis estimated an RMSE increase of 0.481 mmol/L per additional 30 minutes (95% CI 0.213‐0.749), but overlap sensitivity reduced certainty. In the 270-study clinical readiness audit, external validation occurred in 4.0% (10/251), prospective evaluation in 0.7% (2/270), calibration in 4.8% (13/270), decision-curve or net-benefit analysis in 2.6% (7/270), and implementation or human-factors evaluation in 2.6% (7/270). Conclusions: Glycemic prediction studies show forecasting and discrimination signals, but heterogeneity, high risk of bias, incomplete uncertainty reporting, and limited external and prospective validation preclude deployable benchmarks. Pooled estimates should be viewed as summaries of analyzable literature. Future studies need transparent horizon, threshold, calibration, validation, uncertainty, and implementation reporting. Trial Registration: PROSPERO CRD420261366978; https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261366978
title: Machine Learning Models for Glycemic Prediction in Type 1 and Type 2 Diabetes: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

summary: Background: Accurate interpretation of pancreatic cancer status and resectability-related information, together with effective perioperative communication, remains a major challenge in pancreatic cancer care. In routine practice, unstructured computed tomography (CT) reports and complex clinical information may limit the accessibility and consistency of clinical information delivery and increase the communication burden on clinicians. Large language models (LLMs) offer new opportunities for clinical information support; however, existing applications are often task-specific and rarely combine CT report interpretation with perioperative consultation within a unified patient-oriented framework. Objective: This study aimed to develop and retrospectively evaluate PancreaGuide, a knowledge-augmented LLM agent designed to support clinician-supervised CT report-based interpretation of pancreatic cancer resectability-related information and standardized perioperative consultation. Methods: We developed PancreaGuide, an agent-based framework integrating structured prompting, retrieval-augmented generation, and a domain-specific pancreatic surgery knowledge base to support clinical information interpretation and perioperative consultation. A retrospective cohort of 444 patients who underwent contrast-enhanced CT at West China Hospital between 2023 and 2025 was analyzed. Three LLMs, ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and Gemini, were evaluated in both base and PancreaGuide-integrated configurations. CT report-based interpretation of resectability-related information was evaluated using accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, negative predictive value, -score, receiver operating characteristic curves (ROCs), and decision curve analysis (DCA) using a surgery-based proxy reference. Perioperative consultation quality was evaluated across 5 dimensions: accuracy, completeness, consistency, safety, and robustness. Results: Higher classification metric point estimates were observed after integration of the PancreaGuide framework across all 3 backbone models. In CT report-based interpretation of resectability-related information, Gemini+ achieved the highest accuracy of 87.4% (95% CI 0.840‐0.902) and a sensitivity of 95.9% (95% CI 0.927‐0.978). All models showed improved sensitivity and specificity estimates after PancreaGuide integration, with improved agreement between model-generated interpretations and observed surgical management status. ROC and DCA suggested improved discrimination and estimated net benefit using the surgery-based proxy reference. In perioperative consultation, PancreaGuide-integrated models received higher expert-rated scores than their corresponding base models across all 5 evaluation dimensions. Gemini+ achieved the highest overall score (mean 3.88, SD 0.38), followed by ChatGPT+ (mean 3.8, SD 10.36) and DeepSeek+ (mean 3.75, SD 0.35). The greatest improvements were observed in completeness and robustness, with consistent gains across clinical consultation domains. Conclusions: PancreaGuide provides a unified, knowledge-augmented framework for clinician-supervised CT report-based interpretation of resectability-related information and perioperative information support across multiple LLM backbones. The CT-based findings should be interpreted as agreement with observed surgical management status rather than validation against an independently adjudicated anatomical resectability. PancreaGuide may serve as an auxiliary information interpretation framework to improve the accessibility and consistency of clinical information delivery, while it should not replace formal radiological assessment, multidisciplinary evaluation, or clinician judgment. Trial Registration: Chinese Clinical Trial Registry ChiCTR2600119597; https://tinyurl.com/5n72btcb
title: PancreaGuide for Computed Tomography Report Interpretation and Perioperative Consultation in Pancreatic Cancer: Development and Retrospective Evaluation of a Knowledge-Augmented Large Language Model Agent

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> Patient education materials (PEMs) are essential for improving health literacy and clinical outcomes. Although large language models (LLMs) hold promise for optimizing content, their performance in generating new PEMs remains unclear. <strong>Objective:</strong> This study aimed to summarize the current evidence on LLMs in generating new PEMs, evaluate readability, quality, and usability in various health care settings, and guide future research and practice. <strong>Methods:</strong> This review followed PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews) guidelines. A comprehensive literature search was conducted in PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, and Scopus from January 1, 2000, to January 1, 2026. Eligible studies were English-language original research studies that evaluated new PEMs generated by LLMs in health care using information assessment tools. Two reviewers independently screened records and extracted data. We conducted a quantitative analysis of the characteristics of the included literature. Furthermore, we classified the PEMs based on core educational tasks and clinical scenarios, and compared their readability, quality, and usability. <strong>Results:</strong> Thirty studies were included, including 11 LLMs and more than 30 diseases; most compared multiple LLMs and used a single prompt. PEMs were classified into 5 categories: perioperative patient education (n=8), chronic disease management education (n=6), specialty disease diagnostic and therapeutic education (n=9), pharmacotherapy safety and adherence education (n=3), and public health and prevention education (n=4). In terms of readability, only 3 records achieved a sixth-grade reading level. Specialty disease diagnostic and therapeutic education performed relatively well, while chronic disease management education had poor readability. The DeepSeek series demonstrated the most consistent performance. In terms of quality, most records were rated as good or higher. Specialty disease diagnostic and therapeutic education showed a polarized distribution, with both high and low quality ratings. Pharmacotherapy safety and adherence education and public health and prevention education had no poor-quality ratings. The ChatGPT series performed relatively well. In terms of usability, most records performed well in understandability but poor in actionability. Perioperative patient education showed a relatively balanced performance. <strong>Conclusions:</strong> LLMs offer a transformative opportunity for developing effective and high-quality PEMs, but they currently fail to meet health literacy standards, particularly in readability and actionability. Future efforts must shift from performance evaluation to implementation strategies. Only through rigorous validation and equitable deployment can LLMs truly improve patient education. <strong>Trial Registration:</strong>
title: Large Language Models for Generating Patient Education Materials: Scoping Review

summary: Background: Effective communication between clinicians and patients plays an important role in the successful delivery of health care. In geriatric medicine, where multimorbidity, polypharmacy, and functional limitations often make treatment plans complex, AI simplifications of clinical reports into patient-friendly language offer a promising way to improve communication. Objective: This study investigated whether AI could generate patient-friendly simplifications of outpatient reports that were comparable to those authored by human experts. Methods: Gemma-3-27B-it, an instruction fine-tuned open-source large language model (LLM) by Google, was used, and few-shot prompting was applied to enable the generation of patient-friendly simplifications of 64 deidentified geriatric outpatient reports written in German while preserving clinical meaning. LLM-generated simplifications were compared with those produced by 2 medical experts in a blinded evaluation. Quality was assessed using three approaches: (1) embedding-based semantic similarity to the original report, (2) blinded expert review by 2 clinicians, and (3) review by patient representatives, with the latter 2 using a standardized Likert-scale questionnaire. Results: AI-generated simplifications were comparable to geriatrician-authored simplifications regarding semantic similarity (=.02) and were preferred by patient representatives (<.001) as well as one expert reviewer (=.001). Expert reviewers perceived physician-authored simplifications as more complete (<.001), a finding that correlated with text length (<.001). Conclusions: This study demonstrates the feasibility of using LLMs via few-shot prompting to simplify medical reports for improved perceived patient comprehension in geriatric care. Future prospective studies should examine whether such AI-driven simplifications positively impact objective health-related outcomes, adherence, and patient engagement.
title: Patient-Friendly Simplifications of Outpatient Reports Using Large Language Models via Few-Shot Prompting: Blinded Comparative Evaluation

summary: Background: The rapid advancement of generative AI (GenAI) holds transformative potential for clinical nursing practice, yet its integration also brings significant risks and uncertainties. Despite growing discourse on AI in health care, frontline nurses’ firsthand experiences, perceptions, and practical needs regarding GenAI remain largely under-synthesized in the existing literature. Objective: This systematic review aimed to synthesize qualitative evidence to clarify the core themes related to clinical nurses’ perceptions, experiences, obstacles, and requirements when using GenAI in real-world clinical settings. Methods: A systematic search was conducted across 10 electronic databases (PubMed, Embase, CINAHL, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, ProQuest Dissertations and Theses, China National Knowledge Infrastructure, VIP Information, SinoMed, and Wanfang) for records published between January 2018 and June 2026. Eligible studies included qualitative and mixed methods studies involving registered nurses that explored their perceptions and experiences of GenAI in clinical practice. Two independent reviewers (MMW and CYZ) performed study selection, quality appraisal, and data extraction, with disagreements resolved by consensus. Quality was assessed using the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) Critical Appraisal Checklist for Qualitative Research. Extracted data encompassed study characteristics, participant demographics, and GenAI-related contextual factors. Data synthesis followed Thomas and Harden’s 3-phase thematic synthesis: initial inductive coding generated descriptive themes, which were subsequently integrated with the Technology Acceptance Model for Artificial Intelligence in Nursing (TAM-AIN) framework to develop higher-order analytical themes. Certainty in the evidence was evaluated using the GRADE-CERQual (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation-Confidence in the Evidence from Reviews of Qualitative Research). Results: Of the 4350 initially identified records, 13 studies from 6 countries (China: n=6; Saudi Arabia: n=3; United States, Singapore, Australia, and South Korea: n=1 each) met the inclusion criteria, encompassing qualitative data from 234 registered nurses. Three main themes emerged: patterns of nurses’ engagement with GenAI (ranging from passive observation to proactive integration), multidimensional perceived threats to adoption (functional, professional, and accountability-related), and the moderating role of organizational readiness, which influenced whether these threats hindered or facilitated GenAI uptake in practice. The GRADE-CERQual assessment showed moderate to high confidence in all findings. Conclusions: Nurses’ engagement with GenAI ranges from passive observation to proactive integration, accompanied by legitimate concerns about functional reliability, professional role displacement, and accountability ambiguity. The moderating role of organizational readiness further highlights that training, tool optimization, and institutional governance remain critical yet often unmet. These findings necessitate coordinated efforts across workforce development, technological design, and regulatory frameworks. Future research should prioritize the development of clinically validated, context-aware GenAI systems that incorporate human-in-the-loop oversight, ensuring that efficiency gains do not compromise the delivery of compassionate, person-centered care. Trial Registration: PROSPERO CRD420251250664; https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251250664
title: Nurses’ Attitudes and Experiences With Generative AI in Clinical Practice: Qualitative Systematic Review
